description: Your challenge is to create an intuitive tool or application that lets mission planners, educators, and the public compare landing sites and dates quickly, visualizing Sun and Earth positions relative to the horizon to assess power generation potential and direct-to-Earth communication windows.
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app that tells mission planners where and when to land at the Moon's south pole. For any candidate site and any date, it answers two questions hour by hour: is the Sun above the local terrain (power), and is Earth above it (direct radio link)? At the pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, so a single crater rim can cut a solar lander's power for days. Using NASA LOLA terrain and JPL Horizons ephemerides, the tool turns this into clear verdicts: viable, marginal or excluded, and shows what a launch delay of N days changes.
details:
What it does

The app has two modes. Discovery mode is a 4-step guided tour (about 5 minutes) for students and the public: the grazing Sun, terrain hiding it, Earth appearing and disappearing, and a replay of two real missions. Mission mode is for planners: choose sites on a polar map, a landing date, a mission duration and alternative dates, then compare scenarios against adjustable criteria (minimum sunlight, minimum Earth visibility, longest night the batteries can survive, minimum Sun elevation). Views include a 360° horizon panorama, a 3D sky dome, a timeline of light and radio windows, a site-by-delay comparison grid, a 60-day launch feasibility calendar and a period zoom. Any scenario can be shared as a link.

How it works

1. For each site, a Python pipeline computes the terrain horizon (elevation of the skyline every 1° of azimuth) from NASA LOLA digital elevation models.

2. Sun and Earth positions (azimuth, elevation) are retrieved hourly from JPL Horizons for 2025 to 2030 (and for the mission dates of IM-1 and Chandrayaan-3).

3. The browser compares the two at every hour: Sun above, partly hidden (the disc is about 0.5°) or hidden; Earth visible or not. It then derives sunlight and Earth-visibility percentages, the longest night, countdowns to sunset and Earth-set, and a verdict per scenario. Everything is recomputed instantly when the user changes a date or a threshold.

Key results

- Terrain matters: at Malapert, for a 14-day mission from 1 March 2025, sunlight drops from 59% on flat ground to 20% with real terrain, and the longest night grows by 4 days 4 hours.

- Delays matter: with a 48-hour battery limit and a 7-day slip, only Connecting Ridge stays viable among the three Artemis-region sites. Its longest launch window in spring 2025 is 21 March to 5 April (16 days).

- Validation: Chandrayaan-3 predicted sunset 4 September 2023 07:33 UTC, lander put to sleep 4 September 2023. IM-1 Odysseus predicted sunset 2 March 2024, last contact 29 February 2024; the lander tipped on its side at landing, which reduced its power. Our model predicts sunset, not hardware accidents.

Benefits

Site selection for Artemis and commercial landers depends on illumination and communication windows. The tool makes this visible in seconds, without specialist software, and makes the trade-offs of a delay explicit. Discovery mode makes the physics of the lunar pole accessible to students.

Limitations

No atmospheric or hardware effects; no custom coordinates yet (a new site requires rerunning the Python pipeline); the polar map shows sites only, without illumination or slope layers; the Paris comparison uses an approximate solar formula (about 1°).

Next steps

Custom coordinates, average illumination and slope map layers, more historical missions for validation.

Tools

Python (horizon and data pipeline), HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript (no framework, no build step), SVG and Canvas for charts and the 3D dome, Web Audio for the sonification. Hosted on Cloudflare; installable as a Progressive Web App and usable offline.
